articles.title: AI for Good: How the UN uses AI to advance human rights
articles.summary: For Ari, a six-year-old boy with learning difficulties in Jamaica, artificial intelligence (AI) opened the door to something many children take for granted: reading a book in his own language. Thousands of miles away, gold miners in Ethiopia are being screened more quickly for tuberculosis, while communities around the world are breathing cleaner air thanks to faster detection of methane leaks.
articles.content:
Across agencies, the UN is implementing AI tools to help promote peace, security and human rights while spearheading the global conversation around AI governance.

By the book

Tweet URL

Six-year-old Ari in Jamaica has learning difficulties which make it difficult for him to study, but now AI technology is converting existing textbooks into interactive formats personalised to his needs.

“The real impact is what this means for children,” Pia Rebello Britto, UNICEF’s Global Director of Education and Adolescent Development, told UN News. “There are countless more examples like Ari’s, showing what becomes possible when digital learning is designed to reach every child.”

For UNICEF, implementing AI means putting the communities it supports at the centre of its technology development process.

The agency worked with advocacy groups to design its Accessible Digital Textbooks for All (ADT) initiative, which tackles a persistent barrier in global education: inaccessible learning materials for the nearly 240 million children worldwide living with disabilities.

While the programme existed before AI’s rapid rise, today’s AI-assisted version now operates in 17 countries, reaching nearly two million children, with a goal of expanding to 50 countries by 2030. Six countries have already joined this year.

Putting a brake on methane

Methane is one of the gases that is contributing to global warming.

“Everybody – every person, citizen – anywhere in the world who is concerned about climate change must have an interest in slowing down global warming, and fixing methane leaks is the emergency brake,” said UNEP Climate Change Division Director Martin Krause.

Tweet URL

Using satellite data to detect large methane leaks and notify governments and companies, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) has helped prevent the equivalent of 24 million gas-powered cars worth of methane emissions since 2024.

That’s the year UNEP launched the Methane Alert and Response System (MARS), which uses AI to analyse data from 30 satellites to identify methane plumes.

Because AI is 12 to 15 times faster and more accurate than humans at detecting methane leaks, UNEP has issued 7,500 alerts, triggering 42 mitigation actions over the past two years, Mr. Krause said.

Companies often take prompt action to address these leaks, Mr. Krause said, because the alerts help them avoid product loss – a win-win for companies and the environment.

Not only is methane 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide in warming the atmosphere, but fixing methane leaks also reduces the proliferation of harmful smog, which can cause respiratory illness.

“This is not the UN building a task force and discussing a problem and having a meeting. This is real stuff,” Mr. Krause said. “This is happening as we speak.”

TB screening

With assistance from the UN’s World Health Organization (WHO), developing countries are using AI to analyse chest X-rays for signs of tuberculosis (TB), allowing faster screenings in areas with fewer specialists.

“It’s really helping people to move through the sort of diagnostic cascade onto treatment much sooner,” Dr. Vanessa Veronese, a scientist at the WHO’s Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases, told UN News.

Earlier diagnosis also means fewer infectious people in the community, reducing onward transmission – a crucial step towards eliminating TB.

Dr. Veronese pointed to Ethiopia, where gold miners face an increased risk of contracting TB due to dust and silica exposure.

The technology behind early diagnosis is called computer-aided detection (CAD).

Soundcloud

Chief among CAD’s benefits is that it generates a TB likelihood score very quickly, helping overstretched radiologists in low-resource settings, which is important because many die from TB if they do not receive treatment.

In 2021, the WHO officially recommended its use to screen for TB in adults and has since supported developing countries in adopting the technology. WHO provides practical implementation guidance, helps TB programmes calibrate the software and studies health outcomes.

“It really does help overcome these historical barriers around skilled personnel, access, cost, availability – all of these access barriers that prohibit good health,” Dr. Veronese told UN News.

Advancing crisis response

UN agencies are also using AI to detect land mines, assess disaster damage, identify suspicious financial transactions, monitor radioactive contamination and accelerate nuclear fusion research.

But as technology advances, the UN is emphasising equity, human rights and ethics to ensure AI promotes development instead of threatening peace and democracy.

Mr. Guterres has called AI “humanity’s greatest opportunity in the 21st century” and “one of its greatest risks,” stressing the need for inclusive oversight.

“We must ensure AI serves humanity, and not the other way around,” he said.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: How the UN uses AI to improve health, education, and the environment
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The United Nations (UN) is using artificial intelligence (AI) to help solve important problems around the world. AI is a technology that allows computers to learn and make decisions quickly. The UN focuses on using AI in ways that support human rights, health, and the environment.

**What happened** – The UN has started several projects using AI. In Jamaica, AI helps six-year-old Ari, who has learning difficulties, by turning textbooks into interactive lessons made just for him. In Ethiopia, AI helps doctors find signs of tuberculosis (TB) faster by analyzing chest X-rays. The UN’s Environment Programme uses AI to spot dangerous methane gas leaks from space, which helps reduce pollution.

**Impact** – These projects show how AI can make a real difference. Nearly two million children in 17 countries now have better learning materials thanks to the UN’s Accessible Digital Textbooks for All program. Faster TB detection helps save lives by getting treatment to patients sooner and stopping the disease from spreading. Detecting methane leaks quickly prevents pollution that warms the planet and harms people’s lungs. These efforts improve health, education, and the environment for millions of people.

**What's next step** – The UN plans to expand these AI projects. The textbook program aims to reach 50 countries by 2030. The methane alert system will keep monitoring leaks worldwide to help governments and companies act faster. The World Health Organization will continue supporting countries in using AI for TB screening. The UN also wants to guide the safe and fair use of AI to protect human rights and peace.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN is using AI in smart ways to help children learn, fight disease, and protect the environment, showing how technology can improve lives globally.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment l'ONU utilise l'IA pour améliorer la santé, l’éducation et l’environnement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Nations Unies (ONU) utilisent l’intelligence artificielle (IA) pour résoudre des problèmes importants dans le monde. L’IA est une technologie qui permet aux ordinateurs d’apprendre et de prendre des décisions rapidement. L’ONU se concentre sur l’utilisation de l’IA pour soutenir les droits humains, la santé et l’environnement.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’ONU a lancé plusieurs projets utilisant l’IA. En Jamaïque, l’IA aide Ari, un garçon de six ans avec des difficultés d’apprentissage, en transformant les manuels scolaires en leçons interactives adaptées à ses besoins. En Éthiopie, l’IA aide les médecins à détecter plus rapidement la tuberculose (TB) en analysant les radiographies pulmonaires. Le Programme des Nations Unies pour l’environnement utilise l’IA pour repérer les fuites dangereuses de méthane depuis l’espace, ce qui aide à réduire la pollution.

**Impact** – Ces projets montrent comment l’IA peut faire une vraie différence. Près de deux millions d’enfants dans 17 pays bénéficient désormais de meilleurs supports éducatifs grâce au programme Accessible Digital Textbooks for All. La détection rapide de la tuberculose sauve des vies en permettant un traitement plus rapide et en stoppant la propagation de la maladie. La détection rapide des fuites de méthane prévient une pollution qui réchauffe la planète et nuit aux poumons des personnes. Ces actions améliorent la santé, l’éducation et l’environnement pour des millions de personnes.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU prévoit d’élargir ces projets d’IA. Le programme de manuels scolaires vise à atteindre 50 pays d’ici 2030. Le système d’alerte au méthane continuera de surveiller les fuites dans le monde entier pour aider les gouvernements et les entreprises à agir plus vite. L’Organisation mondiale de la santé soutiendra les pays dans l’utilisation de l’IA pour le dépistage de la tuberculose. L’ONU souhaite aussi guider l’utilisation sûre et équitable de l’IA pour protéger les droits humains et la paix.

**À retenir en une phrase** – L’ONU utilise l’IA de façon intelligente pour aider les enfants à apprendre, combattre les maladies et protéger l’environnement, montrant comment la technologie peut améliorer des vies dans le monde entier.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo la ONU usa la IA para mejorar la salud, la educación y el medio ambiente
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las Naciones Unidas (ONU) están usando la inteligencia artificial (IA) para ayudar a resolver problemas importantes en todo el mundo. La IA es una tecnología que permite a las computadoras aprender y tomar decisiones rápidamente. La ONU se enfoca en usar la IA para apoyar los derechos humanos, la salud y el medio ambiente.

**Qué pasó** – La ONU inició varios proyectos con IA. En Jamaica, la IA ayuda a Ari, un niño de seis años con dificultades de aprendizaje, convirtiendo libros en lecciones interactivas hechas a su medida. En Etiopía, la IA ayuda a los médicos a detectar la tuberculosis (TB) más rápido al analizar radiografías de pecho. El Programa de Medio Ambiente de la ONU usa IA para detectar fugas peligrosas de metano desde el espacio, lo que ayuda a reducir la contaminación.

**Impacto** – Estos proyectos muestran cómo la IA puede hacer una diferencia real. Casi dos millones de niños en 17 países ahora tienen mejores materiales educativos gracias al programa Accessible Digital Textbooks for All. La detección rápida de la TB salva vidas al permitir un tratamiento más pronto y evitar que la enfermedad se propague. Detectar fugas de metano rápido previene contaminación que calienta el planeta y daña los pulmones. Estos esfuerzos mejoran la salud, la educación y el ambiente para millones de personas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La ONU usa la IA de manera inteligente para ayudar a niños a aprender, combatir enfermedades y proteger el medio ambiente, mostrando cómo la tecnología puede mejorar vidas en todo el mundo.

articles.title: New initiative launched to shield terrorism victims from online harm
articles.summary: The UN has launched a new initiative to protect victims of terrorist attacks from online harm and re-traumatisation, drawing on harrowing survivor accounts, from the Nova Music Festival in Israel to an attack on a FIFA World Cup final viewing party in Uganda.
articles.content:
The initiative was launched at an event on Friday marking the International Day of Remembrance of and Tribute to the Victims of Terrorism.

“It's not just another date on the calendar,” Saynab Warsame, who survived a terrorist attack in Somalia, said in a message to the UN commemorative event. “It's a day that reminds me of who I lost, who I am and who I am still becoming.”

Acts of terrorism kill and maim thousands of people every year around the world, and online harm has been reported by survivors in every region.

“In today's digital world, memories are fragile,” Ms. Warsame said. “With fake videos and information, the truth can easily be lost or changed.”

To address that, the new victim-led initiative was launched by the Victims of Terrorism Associations Network, established by the UN Counter-Terrorism Office last year to drive collective action to support their rights and needs.

Watch the UN Headquarters event here:

‘Tragically, I am not unique’

Rachel Goldberg-Polin is a dual national of the United States and Israel whose 23-year-old son, Hersh, was among more than 250 people captured during the 2023 Hamas attack at the Nova Music Festival in Israel. He was held hostage in Gaza for 328 days before being killed.

“Tragically, I am not unique,” she told the UN event. “There are millions of parents around the world who have had to bury their children.”

She said two human instincts – love and destruction – are “woven into our DNA”, recalling prescient discussions 94 years ago between leading scientist Albert Einstein and psychoanalysis pioneer Sigmund Freud that remain just as salient today.

“Civilisation has to decide whether to rise to the challenge to continually contain our natural tendencies towards war or to give into that slavery of selfish interest even though…it only serves the powerful few,” she said.

“May we use our wisdom, strength and light to do what is right. The choice is hard, but the choice is ours.”

UN Photo/Eskinder Debebe

World Cup nightmare

The scene was a watch party for the FIFA World Cup finals in 2010 in Uganda, when in the 78th minute, two suicide bombers detonated their explosives: more than 70 people were killed and many others injured – including Hassan Ndugwa.

That night became a call to action for him – to recover and also join the fight to prevent the spread of violent extremism.

Angered by the misrepresentation of Islam in the aftermath of the attacks, he and another survivor founded the Uganda Muslim Youth Development Forum, which has already reached thousands of young people through job skills programmes and other support.

UN Photo/Eskinder Debebe

‘Seeing a brighter future’

“The most fulfilling work that we have done since then is the work to provide alternatives to youth,” Mr. Ndugwa told UN News.

“They are seeing a bright future. They now have renewed hope. So, it’s difficult for you to come and tell them to join an extremist group because they are…seeing a brighter future.”

The forum continues to push back on violent extremism and promote peace through religious and community engagement, he said.

He also underlined the importance of survivor voices and the role of remembrance in healing.

Listen to the full interview here:

Soundcloud

United against terror

Echoing that sentiment, UN Secretary-General António Guterres paid tribute to victims and survivors.

“This year’s theme, Healing through memory, reminds us that remembrance is a pathway to recovery and renewal,” he told the commemoration. “But, how we remember matters.”

He said victims’ stories must never be exploited or used to sow more hate, including on digital platforms.

“Instead of letting terror divide us, we can and must stay united,” he said. “Today and every day, let us stand in solidarity with victims and survivors and build a future free from violence and fear.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: UN launches new effort to protect terrorism victims from online harm
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Terrorist attacks cause pain and loss around the world. Survivors often face more harm online, like fake videos or hurtful messages that can make their suffering worse. The United Nations (UN) wanted to find a way to help protect these victims from being hurt again on the internet.

**What happened** – On the International Day of Remembrance for Victims of Terrorism, the UN started a new project to shield survivors from online harm. This project is led by victims themselves, through a group called the Victims of Terrorism Associations Network. They shared stories from survivors, such as a mother who lost her son in an attack at a music festival in Israel and a man who survived a bombing during the 2010 FIFA World Cup final viewing in Uganda.

**Impact** – The project is important because it listens to survivors and respects their experiences. It helps stop false information and online attacks that can hurt victims again. For example, in Uganda, survivors started programs to give young people hope and keep them away from violence. By focusing on healing and truth, the initiative aims to support victims and prevent more harm.

**What's next step** – The UN and the Victims of Terrorism Associations Network will continue to work with survivors worldwide to improve protection online. They want to spread awareness, help more victims speak out safely, and encourage communities to stand together against hate and violence.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN’s new initiative uses survivor voices to protect victims of terrorism from online harm and promote healing worldwide.

articles.title: The everyday guardians: Rana Tharu women’s implicit roles in Nepal
articles.summary: In this month's Narrative Spotter, we explore an implicit narrative shared through the everyday dynamics of the Rana Tharus in Nepal.
articles.content:
This story is part of Undertones, Global Voices’ Civic Media Observatory’s newsletter and column. Subscribe to Undertones here. It is also part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In 2007, the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, establishing an important framework for advancing and protecting the rights of Indigenous peoples. A central component of the Declaration is protecting Indigenous peoples’ distinct identities and cultural integrity. This includes rights such as practicing, revitalizing, and transmitting cultural institutions, traditions, and customs.

Self-determination is another fundamental principle of the 2007 UN Declaration. It recognizes Indigenous peoples’ longstanding traditions of self-government, autonomous decision-making, and institutional self-reliance, and affirms their right to determine their own political, economic, social, and cultural priorities and to be their own custodians.

In the villages of Kailali and Kanchanpur in Nepal’s far-western Terai, through language, traditional attire, ancestral jewelry, songs, rituals, and food systems, Rana Tharu women share a distinct cultural identity at a time when migration, urbanization, and social change threaten many Indigenous traditions — setting an implicit narrative that gives women a critical role in preserving Rana Tharu cultural heritage.

Narrative: Women are essential custodians of Rana Tharu cultural heritage

For many children, their first introduction to the Rana Tharu language comes from their mothers and grandmothers. Household conversations, lullabies, wedding songs, and folk tales remain important spaces where the language survives and flourishes.

As formal education and media increasingly prioritize Nepali and English, women often become the last line of defense preventing the loss of local languages. Elders pass on stories about ancestors, forests, farming, and community life to younger generations, keeping language connected to culture and memory.

Rana Tharu women’s role as culture custodians goes beyond language preservation. In a YouTube video by Ranatharu.com, Sarswati Rana congratulates Rambeti Rana, a winner of a Teej song competition. Rambeti Rana wears traditional attire in the video. Rana Tharu textiles feature intricate floral and abstract embroidery, colorful pom-poms, tassels, and creative patchwork. These vibrant elements showcase the community’s artistic traditions, resourcefulness, beliefs, rituals, and strong connection to nature and wildlife. Each design carries cultural meaning and tells a story passed down through generations largely by women. The jewelry that accompanies the dress reflects the Rana Tharu community’s longstanding connections across the region that now includes Nepal and northern India. Each piece carries stories of trade, migration, family lineage, and cultural continuity.

Jeevan Rana, Vice-Chairperson, Provincial Policy and Planning Commission, Sudurpashchim Province, when asked about traditional attire, told Global Voices that:

The traditional clothes of Rana Tharu women and men is far more than clothing it is a living expression of our identity, history, and collective memory. By wearing and preserving these traditional garments, we honor our roots and pass on the rich cultural legacy of the Rana Tharu community to future generations.

In the video, Rambeti Rana sings a Teej song traditionally performed by women during the Hindu festival of Teej. Among the Rana Tharu, women observe the Teej fast for the health, prosperity, and long life of their brothers and nephews. This practice differs from that of most other Hindu communities, where women traditionally fast for the well-being and longevity of their husbands or in the hope of finding an ideal husband.

The narrative positioning women at the center of tradition-passing is asserted mostly through actions and, implicitly, in the everyday dynamics and expressions of the Rana Tharu community.

Rana Tharu Hori (Holi) celebrations offer another important cultural space where women express and celebrate their heritage through clothing and actions. Regarded as the community’s grandest festival, Hori is distinguished by its duration of more than 38 days and its distinct phases. The celebrations begin with Zinda Hori, meaning “living Hori,” which marks the start of this elaborate festive period.

The context surrounding the narrative

Rana Tharus are a distinct community within Nepal’s broader Tharu population, concentrated primarily in the Terai region. They are one of five major Tharu groups found predominantly in Nepal, alongside the Kathariya, Dangaura, Chitwan (Chitwaniya), and Kochila Tharu. Of these groups, the Kochila are the most geographically widespread.

Rana Tharus traditionally claim Rajput ancestry and migration from Chittorgarh, India, though some scholars dismiss this and assert the myth originates from “caste climbing” storytelling.

Whether Rana Tharus’ origins are factually from Chittorgarh, India, or not, the community’s collective memory holds to the claim of Rajput ancestry, carried by women who fled to Sukala, today’s Shuklaphanta, Terai, Nepal, after Muslims invaded Chittorgarh, India. According to Lai Ming Lam’s publication “Land, Livelihood and Rana Tharu Identity Transformations In FarWestern Nepal,” Rana Tharu oral shared history document that, “there was one Brahmin girl in the group and she fell in love with one of the retainers” one of the servants of the king who was also fleeing and that as a consequence of her higher caste status, “it was agreed that her husband could never enter the kitchen when she made food,” placing women in a higher status.

Beyond preserving language, dress, jewelry, and food traditions, Rana Tharu women play a central role in maintaining religious and ritual life. Their responsibilities extend to agricultural rituals tied to sowing, planting, and harvesting, where prayers and offerings seek fertility, prosperity, and protection for crops and livestock. Women also oversee regular weekly worship, seasonal deity services, and periodic family ceremonies, including traditional three-year deity rituals that reaffirm ancestral and spiritual bonds.

From the 1950s to the 1970s, government resettlement programs and migration into Nepal’s western Terai significantly changed landownership and settlement patterns. Many Rana Tharu families lost customary landholdings as migrants acquired land, while the creation and later expansion of Shuklaphanta Wildlife Reserve displaced households from ancestral settlements and farmland.

Inheritance-driven land fragmentation is a major challenge for the Rana Tharus. As land is divided among sons and later among brothers and their descendants, farms become smaller and less economically viable. Combined with land loss and population growth, this fragmentation has weakened the community’s agricultural base, reduced farm productivity, and increased dependence on wage labor, migration, and other non-agricultural livelihoods.

Education has also been a long-term challenge for Rana Tharus. Historically, limited access to education and the priority given to agriculture and immediate economic needs restricted educational advancement. Although education is increasingly valued today, these historical disadvantages remain visible in the relatively low representation of Rana Tharus in higher education, government service, professional occupations, and decision-making institutions, limiting their political and administrative influence.

Restrictions on forests, grazing lands, wetlands, and other communal resources have disrupted traditional livelihoods and crafts of Rana Tharus. Reduced access to timber, bamboo, reeds, grasses, and other materials has made practices such as basket weaving, household-item production, and traditional house construction increasingly difficult.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the vital role of Rana Tharu women in preserving Indigenous cultural heritage, language, traditions, and identity amidst social and environmental challenges. It emphasizes Indigenous rights, cultural continuity, and self-determination, which have broad significance for Indigenous communities and human rights globally. The story provides detailed context on cultural practices, challenges, and the importance of women as custodians, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news with meaningful social impact.
articles.personality_title: Rana Tharu women keep Nepal’s Indigenous culture alive through everyday traditions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Rana Tharu are an Indigenous community living in Nepal’s far-western Terai region. Like many Indigenous groups, they face challenges from land loss, migration, and social change. Protecting their culture, language, and traditions has become harder over time.

**What happened** – In their villages, Rana Tharu women play a key role in preserving their culture. They teach the community’s language to children through daily conversations, lullabies, and stories. Women also keep traditional clothing, jewelry, songs, and rituals alive. For example, women perform special songs during the Hindu festival of Teej and wear colorful embroidered dresses that tell stories about their history and connection to nature.

**Impact** – This story shows how women are the main keepers of Rana Tharu culture at a time when many traditions risk fading away. Their role helps the community maintain its identity and pass it to the next generation. Women’s work supports not just language and art but also important religious and farming rituals that connect people to their land and ancestors.

**What's next step** – As the community faces ongoing changes, supporting education and protecting land rights will be important to strengthen these cultural traditions. Recognizing and valuing women’s roles can encourage more efforts to preserve Indigenous heritage and ensure it continues to thrive.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Rana Tharu women in Nepal quietly preserve their community’s language, traditions, and identity through everyday actions that keep their culture strong despite many challenges.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les femmes Rana Tharu préservent la culture indigène du Népal à travers leurs traditions quotidiennes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Rana Tharu sont une communauté indigène vivant dans la région du Terai, à l’extrême ouest du Népal. Comme beaucoup de peuples indigènes, ils font face à des défis liés à la perte de terres, à la migration et aux changements sociaux. Protéger leur culture, leur langue et leurs traditions devient de plus en plus difficile.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Dans leurs villages, les femmes Rana Tharu jouent un rôle central dans la préservation de leur culture. Elles transmettent la langue aux enfants par des conversations quotidiennes, des berceuses et des histoires. Elles maintiennent aussi vivants les vêtements traditionnels, les bijoux, les chants et les rituels. Par exemple, les femmes chantent lors du festival hindou Teej et portent des robes brodées colorées qui racontent leur histoire et leur lien avec la nature.

**Impact** – Cette histoire montre que les femmes sont les gardiennes principales de la culture Rana Tharu à une époque où beaucoup de traditions risquent de disparaître. Leur rôle aide la communauté à conserver son identité et à la transmettre aux générations futures. Le travail des femmes soutient non seulement la langue et l’art, mais aussi des rituels religieux et agricoles importants qui relient les gens à leur terre et à leurs ancêtres.

**Prochaine étape** – Face aux changements continus, soutenir l’éducation et protéger les droits fonciers sera important pour renforcer ces traditions culturelles. Reconnaître et valoriser le rôle des femmes peut encourager davantage d’efforts pour préserver le patrimoine indigène et assurer sa continuité.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les femmes Rana Tharu au Népal préservent discrètement la langue, les traditions et l’identité de leur communauté grâce à des actions quotidiennes qui maintiennent leur culture vivante malgré les nombreux défis.
articles.personality_title_es: Las mujeres Rana Tharu mantienen viva la cultura indígena de Nepal con sus tradiciones diarias
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Rana Tharu son una comunidad indígena que vive en la región del Terai, al suroeste de Nepal. Como muchos pueblos indígenas, enfrentan desafíos por la pérdida de tierras, la migración y los cambios sociales. Proteger su cultura, idioma y tradiciones se ha vuelto más difícil con el tiempo.

**Qué pasó** – En sus aldeas, las mujeres Rana Tharu juegan un papel clave en la preservación de su cultura. Enseñan el idioma a los niños mediante conversaciones diarias, canciones de cuna e historias. También mantienen vivas la ropa tradicional, las joyas, las canciones y los rituales. Por ejemplo, las mujeres cantan durante el festival hindú Teej y usan vestidos bordados y coloridos que cuentan historias sobre su historia y su conexión con la naturaleza.

**Impacto** – Esta historia muestra cómo las mujeres son las principales guardianas de la cultura Rana Tharu en un momento en que muchas tradiciones corren riesgo de desaparecer. Su papel ayuda a la comunidad a mantener su identidad y a transmitirla a las nuevas generaciones. El trabajo de las mujeres sostiene no solo el idioma y el arte, sino también rituales religiosos y agrícolas importantes que conectan a las personas con su tierra y sus antepasados.

**Próximo paso** – Mientras la comunidad enfrenta cambios continuos, apoyar la educación y proteger los derechos sobre la tierra será importante para fortalecer estas tradiciones culturales. Reconocer y valorar el papel de las mujeres puede fomentar más esfuerzos para preservar el patrimonio indígena y asegurar que continúe prosperando.

**Resumen en una frase** – Las mujeres Rana Tharu en Nepal preservan silenciosamente el idioma, las tradiciones y la identidad de su comunidad mediante acciones diarias que mantienen viva su cultura a pesar de los desafíos.

articles.title: Why we must stop talking about artificial general intelligence — and instead build ‘pro-worker’ AI
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 21 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02566-6Rather than racing to replace people, we should build AI tools that amplify human expertise and expand opportunity.
articles.content:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping the world in front of our eyes. The concerns around AI, however, extend beyond the uncertainty and disruption that accompany any other radical technological change. They stem in part from the direction AI development has taken: many leading companies are engaged in a single-minded pursuit of artificial general intelligence (AGI).

Why AI hasn’t caused a job apocalypse — so far

AGI is generally understood as an AI system that can match or exceed human capabilities on most economically valuable tasks. In such a world, the automation of work would not be limited to specific industries or routine jobs. Instead, machines would take over many forms of work, including highly skilled professions. The consequences of this displacement of human labour would be unparalleled.

To draw attention to this urgent public-policy challenge, I joined thousands of economists and AI researchers in signing We Must Act Now, a statement urging policymakers and technology leaders to steer AI towards complementing, rather than replacing, human labour.

Studies of the US labour market suggest that, since 1980, automation has played a crucial part in increasing inequality by reducing demand for workers who perform routine tasks (D. Acemoglu and P. Restrepo Econometrica 90, 1973–2016; 2022). The adoption of industrial robots in manufacturing offers a clear example: evidence shows that although productivity has increased, many of the communities most exposed to automation experienced employment and wage declines (D. Acemoglu and P. Restrepo J. Polit. Econ. 128, 2188–2244; 2020).

The dynamic already visible with industrial robots is likely to intensify as AI adoption expands. What is at stake is not only shared prosperity, but also our democratic system. Societies cannot remain stable if large numbers of people are excluded from economic opportunity.

AI is transforming the economy — understanding its impact requires both data and imagination

However, this outcome is not inevitable. Technology does not have a predetermined social purpose, nor does it dictate a single future. This is especially true of AI, which includes a range of technologies. The current focus is on automation: replacing human labour wherever possible.

But there is another path. AI tools can also be designed to complement workers, enhancing their capabilities and productivity, rather than substituting for them. Such a pro-worker approach could deliver gains that are shared more broadly and could include stronger productivity growth.

Take teaching, for instance. Rather than replacing teachers, AI tools could help them to identify areas in which students are struggling and enable teachers to provide more personalized support at scale. Policymakers could encourage this kind of worker-complementing innovation through regulation and targeted incentives.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant and inspiring shift in AI development philosophy, advocating for AI tools that complement rather than replace human labor. This approach promotes economic inclusion, shared prosperity, and democratic stability by emphasizing pro-worker AI that enhances human expertise and opportunity. The story addresses broad societal impact and provides concrete examples and policy suggestions, fulfilling the criteria for good news.
articles.personality_title: Building AI that helps workers instead of replacing them
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing many parts of our lives and work. Some people worry that AI will replace human jobs, especially with a type called artificial general intelligence (AGI), which could do almost any job a person can do.

**What happened** – Experts, including economists and AI researchers, have come together to urge leaders to focus AI development on tools that support and help workers, not replace them. They signed a statement called We Must Act Now to encourage this new approach.

**Impact** – So far, automation has helped machines do routine jobs, which has sometimes led to fewer jobs and lower wages for certain workers. This has made economic inequality worse in some communities. But if AI is designed to work with people—like helping teachers see where students need extra help—it can make jobs better and help more people succeed.

**What's next step** – Policymakers and companies can encourage AI that supports workers by creating rules and incentives. This could lead to new tools that improve how people work and share the benefits of technology more fairly.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Experts are calling for AI to be built as a tool that helps workers grow and succeed instead of replacing their jobs.
articles.personality_title_fr: Créer une intelligence artificielle qui aide les travailleurs plutôt que de les remplacer
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L'intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme beaucoup d'aspects de notre vie et de notre travail. Certains craignent que l'IA remplace les emplois humains, surtout avec un type appelé intelligence artificielle générale (IAG), capable de faire presque tous les métiers humains.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des experts, dont des économistes et chercheurs en IA, se sont réunis pour demander aux dirigeants de concentrer le développement de l'IA sur des outils qui soutiennent et aident les travailleurs, plutôt que de les remplacer. Ils ont signé une déclaration appelée Il faut agir maintenant pour encourager cette nouvelle approche.

**Impact** – Jusqu'à présent, l'automatisation a surtout pris en charge les tâches routinières, ce qui a parfois réduit les emplois et les salaires dans certaines communautés, augmentant les inégalités économiques. Mais si l'IA est conçue pour travailler avec les humains – par exemple en aidant les enseignants à identifier les difficultés des élèves – elle peut améliorer les emplois et aider davantage de personnes à réussir.

**Prochaine étape** – Les responsables politiques et les entreprises peuvent encourager une IA qui soutient les travailleurs en créant des règles et des incitations. Cela pourrait conduire à de nouveaux outils qui améliorent le travail des personnes et partagent plus équitablement les bénéfices de la technologie.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Les experts appellent à construire une IA qui aide les travailleurs à progresser et réussir plutôt que de remplacer leurs emplois.
articles.personality_title_es: Construir una IA que ayude a los trabajadores en lugar de reemplazarlos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La inteligencia artificial (IA) está cambiando muchos aspectos de nuestra vida y trabajo. Algunas personas temen que la IA reemplace los empleos humanos, especialmente un tipo llamado inteligencia artificial general (IAG), que podría hacer casi cualquier trabajo que hace una persona.

**Qué pasó** – Expertos, incluidos economistas e investigadores de IA, se unieron para pedir a los líderes que enfoquen el desarrollo de IA en herramientas que apoyen y ayuden a los trabajadores, no que los reemplacen. Firmaron una declaración llamada Debemos Actuar Ahora para promover este nuevo enfoque.

**Impacto** – Hasta ahora, la automatización ha hecho que las máquinas realicen trabajos rutinarios, lo que a veces ha provocado menos empleos y salarios más bajos para ciertos trabajadores, aumentando la desigualdad económica. Pero si la IA se diseña para trabajar con las personas —como ayudar a los maestros a ver dónde los estudiantes tienen dificultades— puede mejorar los trabajos y ayudar a más personas a tener éxito.

**Próximo paso** – Los responsables políticos y las empresas pueden fomentar una IA que apoye a los trabajadores mediante reglas e incentivos. Esto podría llevar a nuevas herramientas que mejoren el trabajo de las personas y compartan los beneficios de la tecnología de manera más justa.

**Mensaje clave en una frase** – Los expertos piden construir una IA que ayude a los trabajadores a crecer y tener éxito en lugar de reemplazar sus empleos.
